subject: Business
title: The Decoy Effect in Pricing
description: A 60-second lesson on The Decoy Effect in Pricing.

hook.text: Small popcorn: $3. Large: $7. Nobody buys large. Add medium at $6.50 and suddenly large looks like a steal.

buildup.text: The decoy effect adds a third option that makes one of the originals look far more attractive.

discovery.text: The decoy is never meant to be chosen. Its only purpose is to push customers toward the target option.

twist.text: The Economist tested this: web-only $59, print-only $125, web+print $125.

climax.text: SaaS companies use three-tier pricing for this exact reason. The middle tier is often the decoy.

punchline.text: The option you ignore is the one doing all the selling.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the decoy option in pricing?
options: To make the target option look more attractive by comparison
To offer customers a budget choice
To confuse competitors about the pricing strategy

details.summary: The decoy effect introduces a strategically inferior third option that makes one of the original two options appear significantly more attractive. By adding a decoy that is close in price but inferior to the target product, businesses steer customers toward the more profitable option.
details.whyItMatters: The decoy effect demonstrates that preferences are not fixed but are constructed by context. Adding an option nobody chooses can dramatically shift purchasing toward a specific product, making pricing architecture a powerful revenue optimization
takeaways: A strategically inferior third option makes the target option look like the best deal
The Economist's famous pricing experiment showed decoys shift 40 percent of choices
Preferences are constructed by context, not fixed internal values

faq.question: How does the classic Economist subscription demonstrate the decoy effect?
faq.answer: The Economist offered web-only for $59, print-only for $125, and web-plus-print for $125. Nobody chose print-only, but its presence as a decoy made web-plus-print seem like an incredible deal. Without the decoy, most chose the cheap web-only option. The decoy shifted preference dramatically.

faq.question: How can businesses design effective pricing decoys?
faq.answer: The decoy must be clearly inferior to the target but similar in price. It should be asymmetrically dominated, meaning worse than the target on all dimensions but competitive with the other real option. Three-tier pricing is the most common application where the middle tier is the intended choice.
